title: How train events are detected
summary: Trains are detected automatically and appear here right away — no per-event human approval. A calibrated horn detector keeps the page clean; a person only strikes off the occasional false positive. Clip audio is private by default.
method: A microphone about 1,500–1,700 ft from the freight line records the soundscape.
A loose first-pass listens for sustained energy and grabs a candidate clip whenever something might be a train (it over-triggers on purpose — better to look than miss).

A calibrated horn detector then confirms each clip: it needs tonal energy in a narrow band (a horn is near a pure tone; wind, planes, and engines are broadband). Confirmed → the event is published automatically; not a horn → discarded.
Audio comes from a backyard mic, so a confirmed train's clip audio is NOT served publicly unless individually published — the event still shows and counts.
A human reviews the confirmed events out-of-band and strikes off any false positive, which removes it from the page.

accuracy.note: Measured for the calibrated detector against the labeled examples (clips within 5 minutes counted as one train pass). ~1 in 25 shown events is a false positive a human later strikes off; the detector improves as more examples are confirmed.

caveats: Automatic, with a small margin of error: roughly 1 in 25 shown events is a false positive until it's struck off, and a quiet pass with no horn can be missed.
Distance: only the horn carries this far, so counts reflect horn events — not necessarily every train that passed.
One backyard mic: no train direction or speed, and audio can catch nearby conversation — which is why clip audio stays private unless individually published.
Look-alikes: planes and sirens can sound horn-like; the detector pushes them down (planes currently 0 of 50 in testing) but a few slip through and get struck off.
The detector is recalibrated from each new batch of confirmed examples, so the parameters above evolve over time.
